sentences.text: Alamosaurus is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaurs, a name translating to 'Ojo Alamo lizard'.

Adult individuals reached approximately 26 meters in length, stood 5 meters tall at the shoulders, and weighed between 30 and 35 tonnes. Their bodies featured a small head, a long robust neck, and a broad sturdy torso supported by cylindrical legs.
In general appearance, this dinosaur resembled Brachiosaurus more closely than Diplodocus.

Gilmore described the genus in 1922 after discovering the holotype, a left scapula, in June 1921 in New Mexico alongside Reeside and Sternberg. He also described a paratype, a right ischium, from the same collection.
Later, in 1946, Gilmore posthumously described specimen USNM 15560 found in Utah in 1937, though Gregory S. Paul reclassified this specimen as the holotype of Utetitan zellaguymondeweyae in 2025.
This animal is one of the few sauropods known to have survived in North America following a thirty-million-year gap in the fossil record.

Although no skull has been found, rod-shaped teeth likely belonged to the animal. It uniquely possessed pneumatised ribs extending for two-thirds of their length and walked slowly at speeds between 3.2 and 4 km/h without dragging its tail.
The type species is Alamosaurus sanjuanensis, and Friedrich von Huene classified the genus within the family Titanosauridae in 1927.

Alamosaurus lived in southwestern North America during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period, specifically in the Naashoibito Member of the Ojo Alamo Formation dated to approximately 66.87 million and 66.38 million years ago.

Thomas M. Lehman describes the Late Cretaceous fauna in southern North America, dominated by Alamosaurus and Quetzalcoatlus, as representing semi-arid inland plains with a superficially 'Jurassic' aspect. Fossils found in the Evanston Formation in Wyoming indicate it shared its environment with Triceratops.

Some specimens suggest that Alamosaurus may have been larger than the standard estimates. Thomas Holtz hypothesized that the maximum length could be 30 meters or more and weight 72.5 to 80 tonnes, while Scott Hartman estimates Alamosaurus at 28-30 meters based on a tibia, but notes scientists are unsure if that tibia belongs to Alamosaurus or a new species. It is debated whether fossils from formations like the North Horn, Black Peaks, and Javelina belong to Alamosaurus or a distinct genus.
